stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
In a study by geographer Lena Ostrova, volunteers navigated an unfamiliar town using either a folded paper map or turn-by-turn phone directions. Afterward, the paper-map group drew far more accurate sketches of the town's layout. Ostrova concluded that consulting a paper map strengthens a traveler's mental model of a place.

Text 2
Ostrova's results certainly deserve attention. But her paper-map volunteers also took nearly twice as long to finish the route, pausing often at intersections. Those extra minutes spent looking around, rather than the map itself, could have produced their sharper mental pictures.
choices: Consulting a paper map builds a stronger mental model of a place than following phone directions does.
Ostrova's sketch results are unreliable because her two groups of volunteers moved at different speeds.
Volunteers who used paper maps came away with a more accurate sense of the town's layout.
Navigation studies should require every volunteer to finish the route in the same amount of time.
explanation: Text 2 begins by granting that Ostrova's results 'deserve attention.' It does not dispute that the paper-map group drew better sketches. It disputes only the cause: the extra time, not the map, may explain the result. The finding itself, that paper-map users ended up with a more accurate sense of the layout, is the ground both authors share.

A.why: This is Ostrova's conclusion, and it ignores Text 2's caveat. Text 2 suggests the extra time spent looking around, not the map, may have strengthened the volunteers' mental pictures, so Author 2 would not sign on to this statement.

B.why: You read Text 2's 'But' as a full rejection. Text 2 never calls the sketch results unreliable. It accepts them and offers a different explanation. Ostrova, of course, would not call her own results unreliable either.

D.why: Neither author proposes a rule for designing studies. Text 2 points out a difference in timing, but recommending a fixed time limit goes beyond what either text says.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
In a three-year Iowa trial, agronomist Rafael Duarte planted clover between rows of corn. Because clover adds nitrogen to soil, the interplanted plots needed 30 percent less synthetic fertilizer to match the yields of plots without clover. Duarte concluded that clover interplanting can cut corn growers' fertilizer costs.

Text 2
Duarte's trial offers encouraging evidence that clover can stand in for some fertilizer. Still, all three trial years were unusually wet. In drier regions, clover competes with corn for scarce soil moisture, and the savings on fertilizer may be erased by lost yield.
choices: In Duarte's trial, clover allowed the corn plots to reach their yields with less synthetic fertilizer.
Clover interplanting would lower fertilizer costs for corn growers in nearly every farming region.
Duarte's trial gives little reason to think that clover supplies corn with any usable nitrogen.
The unusually wet weather in Iowa was the main reason the clover plots succeeded in Duarte's trial.
explanation: Text 2 concedes that the trial 'offers encouraging evidence that clover can stand in for some fertilizer,' which is Text 1's finding. It then turns on 'Still' to limit where the finding applies, namely in drier regions. Both authors accept what happened in the trial itself.

B.why: You took Text 2's concession as full agreement and missed the caveat. Text 2 argues that in drier regions the savings may be erased by lost yield, so Author 2 would reject a claim about 'nearly every farming region.'

C.why: This treats 'Still' as total disagreement. Text 2 explicitly says the trial offers encouraging evidence that clover can stand in for fertilizer, and Text 1 states that clover adds nitrogen.

D.why: Text 2 notes that the years were wet but never calls the weather the main reason for the results. Duarte credits the clover's nitrogen, so he would not agree either.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Over several months, astronomer Ines Halvorsen's team watched the star HD 41870 fade by as much as 15 percent in uneven, irregular dips. The fading light also grew redder, a known sign of dust. Because the dips were so irregular, the team concluded that a lumpy disk of dust is orbiting the star.

Text 2
Halvorsen's team has made a convincing case that dust is dimming HD 41870. It's important to consider, though, that the dust need not circle the star at all. A cloud drifting through the space between the star and Earth could produce the same irregular dips.
choices: The dust that dims HD 41870 is gathered into a lumpy disk that travels in orbit around the star.
The star's fading is better explained by changes within the star itself than by any dust.
The reddening of HD 41870's light reveals roughly how far the star lies from Earth.
The irregular dips in HD 41870's brightness are most likely caused by dust blocking its light.
explanation: Text 2 opens by granting that the team 'has made a convincing case that dust is dimming HD 41870.' After 'though,' it disputes only where the dust is: it might be a drifting cloud rather than an orbiting disk. Both authors therefore agree that dust is blocking the star's light.

A.why: This is Text 1's final conclusion, and it is exactly what Text 2 qualifies. Author 2 says the dust 'need not circle the star at all,' so you ignored the caveat.

B.why: You read the pivot as a complete rejection. Text 2 calls the case for dust 'convincing.' It never suggests the dimming comes from the star itself.

C.why: Text 1 mentions reddening only as a sign of dust, and neither text connects it to the star's distance. This choice latches onto an incidental detail and misses the point the authors share.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
In 2021, the city of Linden replaced the asphalt on twelve residential streets with permeable concrete, a porous material that lets rainwater soak through to the gravel below. Over the next two summers, storm runoff from those streets fell by more than half. City engineer Paulo Brandt therefore concluded that permeable concrete is an effective defense against street flooding.

Text 2
The early results from Linden are impressive. Over time, however, grit and leaf debris settle into the material's pores. Without regular vacuum sweeping, drainage through permeable concrete has been found to slow sharply within five to eight years.
choices: Permeable concrete will keep Linden's streets from flooding for decades with very little upkeep.
Newly installed permeable concrete can sharply reduce the storm runoff from residential streets.
The drop in runoff measured in Linden was too small to justify replacing the asphalt streets.
Summer storms are the leading cause of flooding on the residential streets of Linden.
explanation: Text 2 grants that 'the early results from Linden are impressive.' After 'however,' it adds a longer time frame in which clogging slows drainage. Neither author disputes that new permeable concrete cut runoff sharply, so that is the point they share.

A.why: You kept the concession and dropped the caveat. Text 2 warns that without regular sweeping, drainage slows sharply within five to eight years, so Author 2 would reject 'decades with very little upkeep.'

C.why: This treats 'however' as full disagreement. Text 2 calls the early results 'impressive' and never questions whether the drop in runoff was large enough.

D.why: Text 1 mentions summers only as the period when runoff was measured. Neither author identifies the leading cause of Linden's flooding, so this choice fixes on an incidental detail.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Over two winters, ornithologist Mae Okonkwo tracked banded black-capped chickadees in Wisconsin woodlands. Birds with access to backyard feeders survived the season at markedly higher rates than birds in areas without feeders. Okonkwo concluded that winter feeding is a reliable way for homeowners to help wild songbirds.

Text 2
Okonkwo's survival data certainly offer encouraging insight. But chickadees snatch a seed and leave. House finches, by contrast, linger in crowds at feeders, where a contagious eye infection passes easily between birds. For finches, a feeder may do as much harm as good.
choices: Winter feeders improve the survival of most of the songbird species that make use of them.
The chickadees' higher survival near feeders was more likely due to disease than to feeding.
Access to winter feeders appears to have helped the chickadees in Okonkwo's study survive.
House finches spend far more time gathered at backyard feeders than chickadees do.
explanation: Text 2 credits Okonkwo's data as 'encouraging insight' and does not challenge what happened to the chickadees. After 'But,' it narrows the claim's scope by naming a species, the house finch, for which feeders may not help. The chickadee result is what both authors accept.

A.why: This repeats Text 1's broad conclusion about songbirds and ignores Text 2's limit. Author 2 argues that for house finches a feeder may do as much harm as good, so they would not agree.

B.why: You read 'But' as a dismissal of Okonkwo's findings. Text 2 raises disease only for finches and never questions why the chickadees survived.

D.why: Only Text 2 discusses how long finches linger, and Text 1 says nothing about it. A point raised by just one author does not describe what both would agree on.
